Upper Mattaponi Indian Tribe

The Upper Mattaponi Tribe describes a living community centered in King William County. Its history and school-foundation accounts connect Adamstown, education and cultural gatherings, while its environmental department explains priorities for learning and stewardship.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Adamstown and the Upper Mattaponi name

The Tribe’s About account traces its community through the settlement called Adamstown and dates the adoption of the name Upper Mattaponi to 1921. It places the community around the Indian View Baptist Church and Sharon Indian School. This specific institutional history should not be collapsed into the separate Mattaponi Indian Tribe because their names share a word.

Read the sources [1] Upper Mattaponi Tribe

02

School, return and community space

The school foundation dates the original school to 1919 and its closure to 1965. It records the building’s return from the county in 1987 and describes its later use for community meetings and cultural gatherings. The Tribe’s About page distinguishes the replacement building of the 1950s from the earlier school. Underlying deeds, interviews and later facility changes need separate review.

Read the sources [2] Upper Mattaponi Tribe [1] Upper Mattaponi Tribe

03

Environmental learning as a public priority

The environmental department brings water, air, fish, mapping, outreach and apiary work into one public mission. It describes combining science with Indigenous Knowledge through community-supported work spanning youth and Elders. These are the department’s stated values and aims; the guide does not infer environmental outcomes or reproduce knowledge that the page does not make public.

Read the sources [3] Upper Mattaponi Tribe

04

A contemporary garden and community food sharing

The Tribe’s Food Sovereignty and Compost Program account places gardens within a continuing farming heritage and dates its garden programme to February 2023. It describes Community Supported Agriculture boxes prepared with produce grown there for Tribal households. This is the institution’s account of food production and sharing, rather than a current distribution announcement or an evaluation of food-security outcomes.

Read the sources [4] Upper Mattaponi Tribe

05

Compost collection through local partnerships

The programme describes collecting compostable waste from local businesses and schools, adding it to onsite piles intended to produce compost for planting crops. Schools appear here as collection partners; the page does not document a particular classroom lesson or learning result. The account connects community food production with waste management, while testing, quantities and later environmental effects remain separate questions.

Read the sources [4] Upper Mattaponi Tribe

06

Training alongside plans for a hatchery

Tricia Andriski’s January 2023 report describes technicians learning at Harrison Lake National Fish Hatchery while the Upper Mattaponi planned a hatchery of its own. The account connects practical learning with the Tribe’s institutional goals, described by Leigh Mitchell. These are reported activities and aims at that date, not proof that a later facility opened or ecological conditions improved.

Read the sources [5] U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service

07

A participant’s interest in outreach and teaching

Johnathan Oxendine, identified in that report as a Haliwa-Saponi participant, describes outreach and environmental education as possible directions for his work. His individual aspirations add a learning perspective to the partnership account. Employment with the Upper Mattaponi does not make all participants citizens of that Tribe, and the report does not establish later careers or measured teaching results.

Read the sources [5] U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service

08

An attributed public perspective on heritage and responsibility

In his 2008 foreword, Kenneth F. Adams links respect for Virginia Indian history with environmental responsibility and the Creator. Credited as Upper Mattaponi, he argues for a history extending beyond the colonial period. These are his published perspectives, not a uniform community creed.

Read the sources [6] Virginia Foundation for the Humanities and Public Policy

09

School and church in a shared institutional history

The guide’s Upper Mattaponi account describes church services in the one-room school before a church was built in 1942. It connects educational and religious spaces without making church participation a condition of identity. This is a dated 2008 account, not a current worship schedule.

Read the sources [6] Virginia Foundation for the Humanities and Public Policy
